classification.difficultyReason: Names three supplied lines using their labelled points.

questions.mappingNote: The response directly assesses naming lines from labelled points, matching geometry-notation.
questions.methodNote: A line is named using any two distinct points on it, in either order. Three non-collinear points determine three lines enclosing a triangular region.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Names three supplied lines using their labelled points.

classification.difficultyReason: Read labelled intersections and parallel markings, and express parallel relationships symbolically.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b directly assess parallel notation; parts c–e apply the accompanying taught definitions of intersection and parallel lines.
questions.methodNote: Name a line using two points, read its intersection with another line, use matching arrow markings for parallel lines, and write parallel relationships with the parallel symbol. Distinct parallel lines have no point in common.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read labelled intersections and parallel markings, and express parallel relationships symbolically.

classification.difficultyReason: Read intersections and parallel marks, then recognise that AC and CB name the same complete line, so their common labelled points are A, B and C.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the definitions and notation taught on pages 2–4. Geometry notation is the closest primary skill; part b additionally assesses parallel-line notation.
questions.methodNote: Name a line using two of its points; identify intersections from common points, parallel lines from matching arrows, collinear points on one line and concurrent lines through one point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read named lines, intersections, concurrency and parallel markings from one supplied diagram.

classification.difficultyReason: Draw explicitly named lines through supplied points and recognise their shared intersection as concurrency; no construction strategy must be devised.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses the geometric language and ruler constructions introduced on pages 3–4; geometry-notation is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Use a ruler to draw the unique straight line through two points. Collinear points lie on one line; concurrent lines pass through one point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct lines through specified points and recognise collinearity and concurrency.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the specified point pairings, label their intersections and check the collinearity already stated in the task.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly applies the line naming, ruler construction, intersection and collinearity conventions taught on these pages; geometry-notation is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Use a straight edge to construct the unique line through two distinct points, label intersections and recognise collinear points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct three pairs of joining lines accurately and label their intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the named lines and choose the direction to extend each until it meets its partner, then label the intersection.

questions.mappingNote: Geometry language and notation is the closest supplied skill: this task constructs named lines and labels their intersections. No angle measurement or algebraic intersection calculation is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Use a ruler to draw the unique straight line through two distinct points. Produce means extend; label the point where two lines meet.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct six lines through specified pairs of points, extend them and label three intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires explaining infinity in two geometric contexts using the definitions of points and lines.

questions.mappingNote: Geometry language and notation is the closest supplied skill. This task assesses the meaning of infinity in geometry rather than naming or symbolic notation.
questions.methodNote: Use the source definitions of a point as a position with no size and a line as straight and extending infinitely in both directions. Explain the unlimited choices of positions on a line and directions through a point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires explaining infinity in two geometric contexts using the definitions of points and lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Systematically distinguishes eight configurations by parallelism and concurrence. Geometry language is the closest listed skill; configuration enumeration has no exact catalogue match.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly uses geometry language and parallel-line conventions. The selected catalogue skill is the closest available match, rather than an exact configuration-enumeration skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the source definitions of distinct lines, parallel lines, intersection and concurrence. Enumerate configurations by parallel families and whether three or four lines meet at one point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Systematically distinguishes eight configurations by parallelism and concurrence. Geometry language is the closest listed skill; configuration enumeration has no exact catalogue match.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the definitions of lines, rays, intervals and opposite rays to four labelled collinear points.

questions.mappingNote: Each response identifies points or common portions of the same labelled line using the definitions on pages 6–7. Geometry language and notation is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: A line extends infinitely in both directions. An interval includes both endpoints and all points between them. A ray includes its first named point and extends forever through its second named point. Opposite rays share a vertex and extend in opposite directions along one line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the definitions of lines, rays, intervals and opposite rays to four labelled collinear points.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish a ray's continuing direction from an interval's endpoints and identify both directions along each line through the specified vertex.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task combines concurrency vocabulary with naming and membership of rays and intervals, best matched by geometry-notation.
questions.methodNote: Concurrent lines pass through one point. An interval contains only the segment between its endpoints; a ray starts at its named vertex and continues in the direction of its second point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise concurrent lines and identify intervals and rays from a labelled diagram.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a labelled line from ordering instructions and identify interval membership.

questions.mappingNote: Naming and constructing a line and interpreting an interval directly assess geometry-notation.
questions.methodNote: Construct the unique line through two distinct points with a ruler. An interval includes its two endpoints and all points between them.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a labelled line from ordering instructions and identify interval membership.

classification.difficultyReason: Name individual angles with the vertex letter in the middle.

questions.mappingNote: Three-letter angle naming directly assesses geometry-notation.
questions.methodNote: Name an angle using a point on each arm and the vertex in the middle; either order of the arm letters is valid.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Name individual angles with the vertex letter in the middle.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify and name every interior angle in a triangle and a quadrilateral.

questions.mappingNote: Listing the angles of labelled figures assesses geometry-notation rather than angle measurement or angle sums.
questions.methodNote: Use the smaller angle between adjacent sides and write its vertex letter between the letters identifying its two arms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify and name every interior angle in a triangle and a quadrilateral.

classification.difficultyReason: Read marked angle boundaries and name each angle with its vertex in the middle.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is naming angles using geometry notation, including whole marked angles crossed by another segment.
questions.methodNote: Use the two rays bounding each marked arc; write the common vertex as the middle letter. Reversing the outer letters gives the same angle. An intervening segment does not divide a single spanning arc into separate requested answers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read marked angle boundaries and name each angle with its vertex in the middle.

classification.difficultyReason: Systematically pair incident edges at each vertex, including the tetrahedron's hidden edge, and name each angle with its vertex in the middle without duplicating reversed names.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess naming angles from labelled incident edges, so geometry-notation is the directly assessed catalogue skill. The measuring-angles teaching beginning below question 7 is outside this exercise.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 introduces rays and their common endpoint. Page 7 names an angle with its vertex in the middle and either order for the outer letters; the smaller angle is intended unless reflex is specified.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Systematically identifies all angles at vertices with two or three incident edges, including a solid.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise four standard angle categories from their marked sectors.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly asks for the size category of its marked angle, matching classify-angles.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of acute, obtuse, reflex and right angles. The arc selects the required sector; a square marks a right angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise four standard angle categories from their marked sectors.

classification.difficultyReason: Find whole-hour clock angles using equal divisions of a revolution.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill is measuring angles in degrees; the actual task uses equal clock divisions rather than a protractor.
questions.methodNote: A revolution is 360°. Divide it into the twelve equal hour divisions. Use the angle at most 180°, as specified by the summary on page 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find whole-hour clock angles using equal divisions of a revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert elapsed time into fractions or multiples of one complete revolution.

questions.mappingNote: Angles at a point is the closest supplied skill for using complete revolutions and their fractions.
questions.methodNote: Use 360° for a complete revolution. The minute hand makes one revolution in 60 minutes; count the full turn travelled, including more than one revolution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert elapsed time into fractions or multiples of one complete revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the correct zero and read a dual-scale protractor for acute and obtuse angles.

questions.mappingNote: Direct reading of the supplied protractor scales matches measure-angles-protractor.
questions.methodNote: Centre the protractor at the vertex, align its baseline with an arm and read the scale beginning at zero on that arm. Check whether the marked angle is acute or obtuse to avoid the supplementary reading.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the correct zero and read a dual-scale protractor for acute and obtuse angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Align a protractor with differently oriented arms, select the correct scale and use each measurement in a subtraction from 360 degrees to obtain its reflex angle.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses protractor measurement in four orientations. Part b uses the same four figures and the taught smaller/reflex distinction, so both parts remain one question.
questions.methodNote: Centre the protractor on the vertex, align its baseline with one arm, and use the scale beginning at zero on that arm. Obtain the reflex angle by subtracting the smaller angle from the 360-degree revolution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Measure four marked angles and subtract each measurement from a revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct specified acute and obtuse angles using a common baseline.

questions.mappingNote: All eight constructions use A as the common vertex and AP as the initial arm; this directly assesses protractor construction.
questions.methodNote: Place the protractor centre at the vertex, align its baseline with the given ray, select the scale starting at zero on that ray, mark the requested angle and draw the new ray.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct specified acute and obtuse angles using a common baseline.

classification.difficultyReason: Measure adjacent angles, combine them and calculate the corresponding reflex angles.

questions.mappingNote: The task begins with protractor measurements; its later responses relate those measurements using adjacent sectors and a full revolution.
questions.methodNote: Measure from the correctly aligned zero scale, combine adjoining sectors and subtract a smaller angle from a 360-degree revolution for its reflex angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Measure adjacent angles, combine them and calculate the corresponding reflex angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Measure intersecting-line angles and identify supplementary and equal pairs.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks students to infer supplementary and equal relationships from measurements; no later vertically-opposite-angle theorem is required.
questions.methodNote: Measure using the correct protractor scale. Angles totalling 180 degrees are supplementary; compare measured angles for equality. A complete revolution is 360 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Measure intersecting-line angles and identify supplementary and equal pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Measure angles at two intersections and compare their sizes using equality and supplementary relationships.

questions.mappingNote: Direct measurement is the main assessed method. Equal and supplementary comparisons use the definitions taught on pages 11–12; later parallel-line proofs are unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Measure with the protractor centre at the vertex and baseline on an arm; choose the correct scale using acute/obtuse size. Compare measurements and use the definition that supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Measure angles at two intersections and compare their sizes using equality and supplementary relationships.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct and measure three rays, identify which ray lies between the others in the student's own drawing, and select the two adjacent angles whose sum gives the outer angle.

questions.mappingNote: The activity checks adjacent-angle addition through a student construction and protractor measurements. The source does not specify which named ray lies between the others; the solution handles every ordering.
questions.methodNote: Centre and align the protractor, select the correct scale, and check that adjacent angles add to their combined angle. State the geometric reason.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct and measure three rays, then check addition of adjacent angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct and measure an adjacent pair, then verify the straight-angle sum.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed conclusion is that adjacent angles forming a straight angle sum to 180 degrees. Protractor measurement supports this check; the sample ray direction and measurements are choices rather than source givens.
questions.methodNote: Use the protractor centre, baseline and correct scale as taught on pages 10–11. Measure both adjacent angles, then add the measurements to check the straight-angle rule illustrated on pages 16–17 and summarised on page 18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct and measure an adjacent pair, then verify the straight-angle sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the prescribed ray directions, measure the three sectors and add the measurements to check the explicitly supplied revolution rule.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed check is the sum of angles at a point; construction and protractor measurement support that check.
questions.methodNote: Use the protractor centring, baseline and scale instructions on page 11. Measure the three adjacent sectors around O and add them, using the revolution rule shown in Example 3 on page 16 and the summary on page 18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct three rays, measure their adjacent angles and check the revolution rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct intersecting lines, measure their four angles and match the opposite pairs to check the stated equality rule.

questions.mappingNote: The principal assessed relationship is equality of vertically opposite angles, established experimentally by construction and measurement.
questions.methodNote: Align the protractor centre with the vertex and its baseline with an angle arm, then select the correct scale. Compare the two vertically opposite pairs at the intersection, as defined on page 17 and summarised on page 18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Draw intersecting lines, measure their four angles and compare the opposite pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify opposite rays at a shared vertex and name the resulting vertically opposite angle.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for angle-pair identification and conventional three-letter angle naming, with Q retained as the vertex.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 defines vertically opposite angles as opposite each other across the intersection vertex; page 18 repeats the corresponding angle fact.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify opposite rays at a shared vertex and name the resulting vertically opposite angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate repeated and algebraic angle labels into equations using right, straight, opposite or revolution relationships, then subtract constants and divide to find each unknown.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b use straight angles; c uses vertically opposite angles; d and e use revolutions; f uses adjacent angles in a right angle; g and h use straight angles. These directly assess finding unknown angles at a point.
questions.methodNote: Use adjacent-angle addition, a revolution of 360 degrees, a straight angle of 180 degrees and equality of vertically opposite angles; give a specific geometric reason.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine equal-angle markings with straight angles, revolutions and vertically opposite angles, giving reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the relevant transversal within rotated and composite figures, then compare the marked angles' interior positions and sides to classify each pair.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses transversal-angle-pair identification; the composite shapes require identifying the relevant transversal.
questions.methodNote: Corresponding angles occupy matching intersection positions; alternate angles lie between the lines on opposite sides of a transversal; co-interior angles lie between the lines on the same side. Recognition does not require parallel-arrow marks.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise the positions of two labelled angles in varied orientations and composite figures.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify which letter strokes act as the transversal and crossed lines, then mark the requested relative angle positions; W requires recognising the alternate pair in a less familiar orientation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b construct alternate pairs in Z and N; c and d distinguish co-interior and alternate pairs in H; e and g construct corresponding pairs in F and E; f constructs a co-interior pair in E; h identifies an alternate pair within W.
questions.methodNote: Identify a transversal and the two lines it crosses. Corresponding means matching relative positions; alternate means interior on opposite sides; co-interior means interior on the same side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct letter diagrams and select angle sectors that satisfy each named relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify three transversal relationships in four differently oriented labelled diagrams.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is identifying transversal angle pairs, rather than calculating angles or asserting equality.
questions.methodNote: Name angles with the vertex as the middle letter. Corresponding angles occupy matching positions at the intersections; alternate angles are interior and on opposite sides of the transversal; co-interior angles are interior and on the same side. Identification does not require parallel markings.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify three transversal relationships in four differently oriented labelled diagrams.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct and measure a pair of alternate angles, then state the parallel-line property confirmed.

questions.mappingNote: The construction and measurement culminate in confirming equality of alternate angles, so parallel-line-angle-properties is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the protractor method on page 11: centre at the vertex, align the baseline with one arm and choose the scale beginning at that arm. Page 23 defines alternate interior angles and states their equality for parallel lines; reasons name the parallel lines.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct and measure a pair of alternate angles, then state the parallel-line property confirmed.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied construction sequence, interpret three-letter angle names when measuring, and connect the equal measurements to the corresponding-angle property.

questions.mappingNote: The measured angles JXS and JYU occupy corresponding positions at the intersections of JK with ST and UV. The final response directly assesses the corresponding-angle property.
questions.methodNote: Construct parallel lines with opposite ruler edges, add and label a transversal, and measure angles by centring and aligning a protractor and selecting the correct scale. Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal; reasons name the parallel lines.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct parallel lines and a transversal, measure corresponding angles, and state the relationship confirmed.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct and label an oblique configuration with A and C on the same side, locate the named angles, and recognise their measured sum as the co-interior supplementary relationship.

questions.mappingNote: The intended conclusion applies the parallel-line angle properties; construction and measurement support that conclusion.
questions.methodNote: Construct parallel lines and a transversal, measure with a protractor and compare with the co-interior supplementary-angle property taught on page 24.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a transversal, measure two angles and identify the parallel-line relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose an intermediate angle connecting the given and target angles, then switch between two marked parallel pairs to build the explicitly requested two-step argument.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess finding unknown angles with parallel lines. Part a uses two co-interior arguments; b and c each use two alternate-angle arguments; d uses alternate then co-interior angles.
questions.methodNote: Use equal alternate angles or supplementary co-interior angles, naming the relevant parallel lines at every step. Page 25 Example 9 models a two-step argument using different parallel pairs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Each part requires two justified steps using different pairs of parallel lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Plan a linked argument by transferring angles between parallels and identifying the remaining region of a straight angle or revolution; part c requires introducing or exploiting a parallel through the target vertex.

questions.mappingNote: Part a combines corresponding angles and a straight angle; b combines a straight angle and corresponding angles; c uses an auxiliary parallel, co-interior angles and a revolution; d uses alternate angles and a revolution. These directly assess unknown angles with parallel lines.
questions.methodNote: Use named corresponding, alternate and co-interior angle properties, identifying the parallel lines; combine these with straight angles and revolutions. Page 31 demonstrates constructing an auxiliary parallel through the required vertex.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines parallel-line angle properties with straight angles or angles in a revolution, giving a reason at each step.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose and orient an auxiliary parallel using the taught construction method, transfer angles to the target vertex, and decide whether to add, subtract or use a straight angle or revolution; part d also requires converting the reflex angle before separating its components.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess construction-based parallel-line reasoning. Original part c omits ABparallelWO. Actual user decision18October2026: addbothmissinggivens andretain70°/45°. The editable partc now explicitlystates ABparallelWO; its constructed alternate-angle derivation gives70°. OriginalPDF/keybytes unchanged; independently reviewthecomplete task.
questions.methodNote: Add a construction line parallel to the given parallels; identify corresponding, alternate or co-interior angles, name the parallel lines, and combine adjacent, straight or revolution angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Students select construction lines and combine several angle relationships, giving reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Each part requires establishing parallel lines from angle evidence before applying a parallel-line angle property.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses alternate angles twice; b uses corresponding angles twice; c uses supplementary co-interior angles twice; d uses alternate angles twice. These directly assess unknown angles involving parallel lines and reasons.
questions.methodNote: First prove parallelism using equal alternate angles, equal corresponding angles or supplementary co-interior angles. Then state the parallel lines when using the appropriate angle property to find the unknown.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Each part requires establishing parallel lines from angle evidence before applying a parallel-line angle property.

classification.difficultyReason: Students select the converse angle condition that makes the named lines parallel, translate the labelled expressions into an equality or supplementary sum, and solve a simple equation.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for the angle value that makes AB parallel to CD, directly assessing converse parallel-line angle properties.
questions.methodNote: Use equal corresponding or alternate angles, or supplementary co-interior angles, to establish parallel lines; state the converse reason.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select a converse angle property and solve a one- or two-step equation to make the lines parallel.

classification.difficultyReason: Students reverse each conditional and independently judge both directions. The rectangle statement requires recognising that one side does not determine area and that a fixed area does not force a particular side length.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 directly applies the statement-and-converse teaching on page 38. The closest catalogue skill includes contrapositive, but this question assesses converses only.
questions.methodNote: Page 38 forms a converse by reversing the condition and conclusion, tests the original and converse separately, and disproves a converse using a counterexample.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form converses and independently test the truth of each original statement and converse. No contrapositive is assessed.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify corresponding and co-interior angles, combine parallel-line and point-angle properties, and give reasons.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c use corresponding angles from page 22; b and e use equal co-interior angles from page 24 and the algebraic example on page 32; d combines page 17 point-angle properties with pages 22–25 parallel-line reasoning.
questions.methodNote: Name the relevant parallel lines with each corresponding or co-interior angle reason. Use vertically opposite angles and supplementary adjacent angles for part d, following the chapter's geometric argument format.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify corresponding and co-interior angles, combine parallel-line and point-angle properties, and give reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Find each complement by subtracting a given angle from 90°.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses complementary angle pairs; no diagram or protractor measurement is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 defines complementary angles as two angles adding to 90°, with the example 30° + 60° = 90°. Find the missing complement by subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find each complement by subtracting a given angle from 90°.

classification.difficultyReason: Find each supplementary angle by a single subtraction from 180°.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess supplementary angle pairs, so angle-pairs-point is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 defines supplementary angles as angles adding to 180°; Example 1 finds a supplement by subtracting the given angle from 180°.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find each supplementary angle by a single subtraction from 180°.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines subtraction from a right angle with subtraction from a revolution.

questions.mappingNote: Finding both unknown angles at O directly assesses unknown-angles-point, supported by right-angle and revolution totals.
questions.methodNote: Use the right-angle definition and adjacent-angle subtraction, as demonstrated in Example 2 on page 16; use the revolution total of 360 degrees taught alongside Example 3 to obtain the reflex angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines subtraction from a right angle with subtraction from a revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine two marked right angles and a given angle using a revolution, then find the reflex angle.

questions.mappingNote: Page 16 Example 3 uses the same four-ray configuration and revolution argument, with a different numerical given. Page 10 defines right and reflex angles; page 15 establishes geometric reasons.
questions.methodNote: Use the marked right angles and the fact that angles in a revolution add to 360°. Subtract the ordinary angle from 360° to obtain its reflex angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two marked right angles and a given angle using a revolution, then find the reflex angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Students identify the sectors making angle AOB and either add them or subtract the other sectors from a straight angle or revolution. These are direct applications of the taught angle totals.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c subtract known sectors from a straight angle or revolution; b and d add adjacent sectors. These directly assess unknown angles at a point.
questions.methodNote: Adjacent angles can be added; a revolution totals 360 degrees and a straight angle totals 180 degrees. Examples 2–4 demonstrate equations with a geometric reason.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine adjacent sectors or subtract known sectors from a straight angle or revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle relationships with adjacent angles, right angles and straight angles.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess unknown angles involving marked parallel lines. Parts a and c transfer the outer angles to the supplied dashed parallel; part b uses the marked sloping parallel pair; part d combines supplementary co-interior angles with the straight extension.
questions.methodNote: Use corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles with parallel lines, followed by adjacent, straight or vertically opposite angles. Page 31 Examples 10–11 explicitly use an auxiliary parallel through a vertex. Part b uses its marked parallel ray and right-angle given, without assuming the triangle angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle relationships with adjacent angles, right angles and straight angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires constructing auxiliary parallel lines and combining several angle relationships across a zigzag.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is finding an unknown angle using parallel lines; the right-angle given supplies an intermediate angle.
questions.methodNote: Page 31 Examples 10 and 11 construct an auxiliary parallel and combine alternate, co-interior and adjacent angles. Page 32 demonstrates setting out geometric equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires constructing auxiliary parallel lines and combining several angle relationships across a zigzag.

classification.difficultyReason: Students introduce auxiliary parallels at two bends, transfer angles, and decide where subtraction and addition apply. Part b repeats the numerical structure symbolically, providing scaffolding for the general expression.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess unknown angles with parallel lines. Part b generalises the numerical reasoning without requiring a more advanced algebraic method.
questions.methodNote: Page 31 Example 10 draws a parallel through a zigzag vertex and adds transferred alternate angles. Example 11 combines auxiliary parallels with subtraction; page 32 combines geometric reasoning and algebra.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies auxiliary parallel-line reasoning first numerically and then to a general symbolic zigzag.

classification.difficultyReason: Students apply the taught auxiliary-parallel construction at two bends, derive a symbolic difference for the middle segment, and combine it with the supplement of gamma. Keeping the angle orientations consistent is the main demand.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is finding an unknown angle using parallel lines; the result is expressed symbolically.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 constructs an auxiliary parallel through a bend and combines alternate angles; Example 11 combines an auxiliary parallel with a straight angle. Page 32 models algebra supported by geometric reasons.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires auxiliary parallel lines and symbolic reasoning across two bends, including the obtuse marked angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must construct and distinguish spatial configurations by parallel pairs and common intersections. The difficult connection is distinguishing a shared line, distinct parallel intersection lines, and a single common point; the supplied case counts guide the classification.

questions.mappingNote: Geometry language and notation is the closest available catalogue skill. The catalogue has no exact skill for enumerating configurations of planes; this mapping does not assert exact taxonomy coverage.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of an infinite flat plane and the chapter's incidence-based classification of parallel, concurrent and non-concurrent objects. Classify the three planes by parallel pairs and common intersections.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires an exhaustive distinction between five incidence configurations of three planes in space.

classification.difficultyReason: Students use the supplied parallel to justify the triangle sum through alternate angles and a straight angle, then extend the explicitly prompted quadrilateral triangulation to five triangles in a heptagon.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses a triangle-angle-sum proof; part b extends it to a quadrilateral; part c extends triangulation to a heptagon, making polygon interior angle sum the most advanced assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use alternate angles on parallel lines and a straight angle to establish part a; use the established triangle result to triangulate parts b and c.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establishes the triangle angle sum using parallel lines, then extends the result through triangulation.

classification.difficultyReason: The hint directs attention to the moving hour hand. Students calculate its fractional turn during fifteen minutes and subtract that turn from the minute hand's quarter revolution.

questions.mappingNote: Finding an unknown angle by subtracting the two turns is the closest available skill; this is neither a protractor task nor a static whole-hour clock task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 9–10 establish a revolution as 360° and a right angle as 90°. Page 16 models calculating adjacent angles; page 32 models an equation for an unknown angle. This challenge extends those ideas to both continuously moving clock hands.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires accounting for the continuous movement of both clock hands.
